newsitem.title: GERMANY: LIFFE, DTB rivalry seen persisting under EMU.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE, DTB rivalry seen persisting under EMU.

text.p: The launch of Europe's single currency will sharpen competition between rival exchanges confronting an increasingly concentrated futures market, top officials at Germany's DTB and London's LIFFE said.

Speaking at a symposium in Frankfurt on Wednesday evening, DTB and LIFFE officials did not rule out more collaboration in the future but underlined their commitment to starkly different trading models.
"Competition serves the market well at present," said Daniel Hodson, chief executive of the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE).
"But I don't rule out friendly conversations with the DTB in future and I don't rule out collaboration."

LIFFE, Europe's top futures exchange, counts the Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB) as its main rival followed by MATIF of France, but sees its supremacy unchallenged by the prospect of European economic and monetary union (EMU), due to be launched in 1999.

The major competitive area would be in interest rate contracts, Hodson said. LIFFE already trades four major contracts in currencies crucial for monetary union -- the mark, lira, sterling and Ecus -- and has a 90 percent market share of contracts with delivery months post-EMU.

"Competitive action from the DTB in relation to the three-month deutschemark contract has not made significant inroads into our market share," Hodson said, adding that London's "open outcry" trading system, as opposed to the DTB's electronic model, gave it a clear advantage.

"No electronic trading system available now or in the foreseeable future can provide the flexibility and speed of the human interface when it comes to the complex combinations, strategies and strips that are the hallmark of STIR (short term interest rate) trading," he said.
German stock exchange chairman and DTB managing director Werner Seifert defended electronic trading, arguing that a "locally anchored" trading system could not meet the demands of a global market.
"Neither LIFFE nor the DTB have finished working out their strategies," he said.
"Both bourses will have to learn that the life span of any trading form is very short."

Seifert said he could envisage LIFFE and the DTB working to set up a joint clearing house in the future. The German exchange also hoped to reactivate its collaboration with MATIF, after last year abandoning a plan to operate a joint electronic system for trading with its French counterpart.
MATIF, he said, might no longer be part of the competitive problem in Europe's futures market, "but it could be part of the solution."
While taking a more reserved line on co-operating with the DTB, LIFFE said it was interested in distributing products developed by other international exchanges.
LIFFE managing director Ralf Herklotz said new products could be developed around reinsurance contracts and that equity-based derivative products should be extended.
